evomod2

Individual-based simulations of the evolution of genetic architecture in multivariate quantitative traits. Genotype-phenotype maps can be additive, multilinear epistatic (one tensor shared by all pairs of loci, or one per pair), a binary ontogenetic matrix (Melo & Marroig 2015) or a contribution matrix (do O & Whitlock 2023); mutation can be a random walk or house of cards; loci can be unlinked or on a genetic map; populations can have discrete generations, overlapping generations or separate sexes with viability selection; and the optimum can be stable, move steadily or fluctuate. The analysis tools split G into its pleiotropic and linkage disequilibrium parts and its additive and epistatic parts, and measure the mutational covariance matrix M. The simulation engine is written in C++ (Rcpp + RcppArmadillo); everything is driven from R.

Documentation and articles: https://diogro.github.io/evomod2/.

evomod2 extends the model of Melo & Marroig (2015, PNAS 10.1073/pnas.1322632112). The Julia package EvoMod.jl is the reference implementation used for prototyping new models and for cross-checking this package.

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("diogro/evomod2")

A C++ compiler is needed (Xcode command line tools on macOS, Rtools on Windows).

Usage

A model combines a genetic architecture, a mutation model, environmental noise, recombination and a life cycle. A population then evolves through a list of selection regimes.

library(evomod2)

# pairwise multilinear epistasis between 50 loci affecting 2 traits
eps <- array(0, c(2, 2, 2))
eps[1, 1, 1] <- 0.05            # positive directional epistasis on trait 1
model <- evomod_model(
  architecture = multilinear(loci = 50, traits = 2, epsilon = eps),
  mutation = mutation(rate = 0.005, cov = 0.05),
  env_sd = 1
)

pop <- evolve(model, n = 1000, record_every = 20, seed = 1,
              regimes = list(stabilizing(2000, omega = 20),
                             directional(2000, delta_theta = c(0.005, 0), omega = 20)))

plot(pop)                 # mean genotypic values and optima
plot(pop, "variances")    # additive genetic variances
trait_means(pop)          # recorded statistics as data frames
variances(pop)
g_matrices(pop)           # G matrices by generation

pop <- evolve(pop, stabilizing(500, omega = 20))   # continue the same population

The other components are chosen the same way, for example:

evomod_model(
  architecture = multilinear(20, 2, epsilon = pairwise_epsilon(20, 2, sd = 1)),  # one tensor per pair of loci
  mutation = hoc_mutation(rate = 0.0005, cov = 0.2),          # house of cards
  env_sd = 1,
  recombination = genetic_map(chromosomes = 2, length = 0.5),
  life_cycle = viability_selection(mates = 2, offspring_per_mate = 2))
fluctuating(5000, every = 10, step = 0.2, omega = 1, structure = list(1:2, 3:4))

Genic and linkage disequilibrium parts of G

For architectures where genotypic values are sums of allele effects (additive(), binary_b()), G splits into a genic part, the G expected without linkage disequilibrium (twice the sum over loci of the covariance of allele effects), and the part due to linkage disequilibrium between loci:

model <- evomod_model(additive(loci = 50, traits = 4), mutation(0.0005, 0.2), env_sd = 0.8,
                      recombination = genetic_map(chromosomes = 2, length = 0.5))
pop <- evolve(model, stabilizing(2000, omega = 10), n = 1000, record_every = 50, seed = 1)
g_decomposition(pop)           # G, genic and ld for the current population
g_matrices(pop, "ld")          # the LD part at every recorded generation

Pleiotropy shows up in the genic part (one allele affecting several traits), while correlations built by selection between loci show up in the LD part (see Melo, Marroig & Wolf 2019 for this decomposition of genetic covariance and its evolutionary consequences).

For any architecture, including multilinear(), the split can be estimated by shuffling alleles among individuals at each locus, which removes associations between loci but keeps allele frequencies (as in do O & Whitlock 2023):

g_decomposition(pop, method = "shuffle", shuffles = 20)

Additive and epistatic parts of G

With epistasis, part of G is not additive. additive_covariance() estimates the additive genetic covariance by least squares, from the state of every locus, for any architecture; G - additive is the epistatic part:

additive_covariance(pop)       # G, additive and nonadditive

Mutational covariance

mutational_covariance() applies single mutations to genomes drawn from the population and measures their effects on genotypic values. It returns the mean effect, the covariance of the effects of one mutation, and the mutational (co)variance input per generation, M. With epistasis or a binary B matrix, mutational effects depend on the genetic background, so M itself evolves:

mutational_covariance(pop, n = 10000)

Matrix statistics

avg_corr() (average correlations within and between modules, and their ratio), autonomy() and mean_autonomy() (Hansen & Houle 2008), eigen_variance() (proportion of variance per principal component), and mean_fitness() and local_effects() for the population itself.

The model

  • Genomes: each allele carries an effect vector in trait space; the effect of a locus, Y_l, is the sum of its two alleles. Effects are measured from the reference genotype (all effects zero), where new populations start unless init_sd > 0.
  • Architectures:
    • additive(): x = Σ Y_l.
    • multilinear(): x = S + Σ_{i<j} ε(Y_i, Y_j) with S = Σ Y_l and a traits × traits × traits tensor ε shared by all pairs of loci (Hansen & Wagner 2001; random_epsilon()), or a different tensor for every pair of loci (Jones, Bürger & Arnold 2014; pairwise_epsilon()).
    • contribution_matrix(): the model of do O & Whitlock (2023), x = C a with weight genes a and contribution genes C as separate loci, used with contribution_mutation().
    • binary_b(): the model of Melo & Marroig (2015). Each allele has a scalar effect y and a column of a binary matrix B saying which traits it affects, x = B y. Used with binary_b_mutation(), which mutates y and the entries of B separately (b_mutation = "random" reproduces the B mutation of the published simulations, which changed entries at half the nominal rate).
    local_effects() gives each locus’s effect in the background of the rest of the genome.
  • Phenotypes: z = x + e, e ~ N(0, env_sd²).
  • Life cycle: discrete generations (wright_fisher(), the default) or overlapping generations (moran(): a generation is n birth-death events, each replacing a random individual by the offspring of two parents drawn in proportion to fitness), or the life cycle of Jones et al. (viability_selection(): separate sexes, females mating with several males, viability selection on zygotes); evomod_model(..., life_cycle = moran()).
  • Mutation: each allele mutates with probability rate per generation (mutation() adds a multivariate normal vector with covariance cov; binary_b_mutation() and contribution_mutation() have their own rates for each kind of gene). A mutation replaces an allele’s effect e by persistence * e + draw; persistence = 1 (default) is a random walk, 0 the house of cards model (hoc_mutation()), for every architecture.
  • Recombination: loci are unlinked by default. genetic_map(chromosomes, length) places loci evenly along chromosomes (Haldane map function), and linkage(rates) sets the recombination fraction between each pair of neighbouring loci; pass either as evomod_model(..., recombination = ).
  • Regimes: drift(), stabilizing(), directional() (the optimum moves steadily) and fluctuating() (the optimum jumps up or down every few generations, all traits together, independently, or in blocks; do O & Whitlock 2023).
  • Each generation: the optimum moves (directional and fluctuating regimes), fitness w = exp(-(z - θ)' Ω⁻¹ (z - θ) / 2) is computed, and the life cycle produces the next generation: with wright_fisher(), every individual mutates and n offspring are produced from parents drawn with probability proportional to fitness; with moran(), n birth-death events; with viability_selection(), matings, zygotes surviving with probability w, and regulation back to n. Offspring inherit alleles through the model’s recombination.
  • Random numbers come from R’s generator: set.seed() or seed makes runs reproducible, and continuing a population gives the same result as a single run.

Extending evomod2

The engine is a set of C++ components declared in src/evomod.h:

Interface Role Implementations
Architecture genome → genotypic value, local effects Additive, Multilinear, MultilinearPairwise, BinaryB, ContributionMatrix
Mutation changes allelic effects GaussianMutation, BinaryBMutation, ContributionMutation
Fitness phenotypes → log fitness GaussianFitness
Recombination parents → offspring genome FreeRecombination, LinkageMap

Regimes and life cycles are handled in the generation loop (evolve_cpp() in src/simulate.cpp).

To add, for example, a new architecture:

  1. Derive a class from Architecture in src/evomod.h and implement genotypic_value() and local_effects() in src/components.cpp.
  2. Add a case to make_architecture() that builds it from the list the R constructor returns.
  3. Write the R constructor in R/architecture.R, returning structure(list(type = "<name>", loci, traits, state_rows, mutation_type, ...), class = "evomod_architecture"). state_rows is the number of rows of a genome (one column per allele): traits for an effect vector per allele, traits + 1 for binary_b(). mutation_type is the mutation model the architecture works with; if the genome needs a special starting state, add it to init_genomes().
  4. Add tests in tests/testthat/ (compare with an explicit, slow R version of the same map), and, for new models, prototype and cross-check against EvoMod.jl.

DEVELOPMENT.md describes the generation loop, the interfaces, random numbers, building and testing in more detail, and AGENTS.md summarises how to use the package for AI coding agents.

Validation

The scripts in validation/ run matching simulations in evomod2 and in an independent implementation, and compare replicate means of G matrices and trait means:

# additive and multilinear models against EvoMod.jl
Rscript validation/cross_check.R path/to/evomod_julia 20
# binary B model against the original C code (lem-usp/evomod, c-gsl; needs GSL)
Rscript validation/cross_check_c.R path/to/evomod/c-gsl 100 8

The C code moves the optimum after each generation and skips the first directional step, so under directional selection its trait means lag evomod2’s by about two generations of optimum movement.
